QUICK TELXIMArHINI). —An ordinary clerk can send a memage of 20 words, including the address, in a minum. This does not seem a very rapid rite of telegraphing, yet if w. consider thateveryaverage English wordeontains Eve letters, and that three separate signals are required by the Morse telegr ph code to indicate a letter, we shill see that 20, or isay'2s words, amount to 375 separate signals, necemilating on the part of the clerk Mg many distinct movements of the hand per minute. Knowing this, we are able to appreciate the rapidity of the operator's manipulation ; still the result Ic distppointing when we take into account the inconeeir- ahle speed at which the electric currents travel along a wire—say 200,000 mile. in a mcond. It is dear that a line It cap.ble of transmitting an enormous number of separate currents in a minuM if sent into it by some rapid niechanical means and heneo we have the automatic sender of the latel Professor Wheatstone, now employed in the postal tele-1 graphs. Wheatstone's apparatus transmits 200 words a minute over some of our luic inland circuits, y , from Leeds to Edinburgh. A still more rapid telegraph was, however, brought quite recently from America, and is now being tried en the Submarine Company's line front Paris to Loudon, for the transmission of Continental ntessagm and Press intelli- gence. It is really a resuscitation of the neglected chemical telegraph of Alexander Bain, the ingenious Caithness clock- maker, and the message is recorded on a travelling tape of chemically.prepared paper by a pair of steel pens or styluses, from which the elm trio Currents ilow and mark the signals M each letter bye double line of blue strokes in the tracks of the pens. This apparatus, which is the praluetion of several united inventor., is now in daily operation in America, on a new line from Boston to Now York, transmit- ting all kinds of messages at the rate of a thousand words a minute. This telegraphic feat will be better appreciated vrhen it is underatood that in order to do this twine 500 mo- rale signal currents are sent into the hoe every secend. Moreover, this instrument can work up to 1,800 words a Indnuteon occasion and under special circumstances. The sending is, of course, done automatically ; the message being tirst perforated on a strip of paper, which is afterwards pulled through an automatic .• key" transmitting currents • •

MC. Joan BILIOHT, PROTECTION.—Mr. John Bright, M.P., writes as follows to Mr. Abraham, the mine, representative in the Rhondda Valley Ido not see what your frien.Ls can to to promote the abolition of • foreign import duties on British productions. What can foreign workmen do to remove any duties we might impose on foreign Prodnetion, aay on wine or tabaceo, or tea or coffee? We can only keep our own t iriff as free as we can, and live in hope that foreign nations will in time find it to their interest to reduce their tariff. I fear one nation can do little for another in matters of this kind. The military system exactions of European Government demand high tax., to sustain them, and high taxation is most easily raised by custom duties, and protection is offerer' to and con- ferred upon manffacturers, who are therefore rendered more pa- lent under high taxation. In America the high tariff comes from the great civil sear. When their debt is greatly reduced, and their taxation becomes much less, they will make tariffs more moderate, and will, by degrees approach free trade. We can best contend against the protection tariffs of foreign countries by adhering faithfully to free trade principles 11l our own tariff..

DMIITCHIN or Cereals BOTCOTT.—Captain Boycott • reached Dublin on Saturday evening. He is attended by detective., ard a epecial oenatable is stationed at his hotel.. A correspondent describing the journey from Ballinrobe In the Irish capital states that when Captain Boycott was recognised in the train be was groaned it. He waa accom- panied in the train by the Assistant Inspector Generaluf , Conetabulary. •nd Mr. Hamilton, R.N. A Inlet engine pre- • ceded the train, and men armed with rifles watched along , the emb.okrnent nearly half the way to Dublin. It is em pected that Captain Boycott will leave Ire Lind in the course of a day or two to- the south of England. It is stated that the cost to the Government of the "Boycott expedition " haa • been £lO,OOO. The Obs^rver states that the first battalion of the linards has received orders to leave for Ireland.

The magistrate. of Clare county met on Saturday asd pas- sed a restolintion calling upon Clio Government to summon Parliament ir. order to obtain such extraordinary powers as shall enable them to deal effectively with a conspiracy an- , precedental in character, and which aims at the total dia- -1 organisation of society. Mr. Michael Ilavitt, addrenfing a land meeting at Sligo on Saturday, adviead hi. hearers to imitate the attitude of the people of ffalliorobe, and Boycott their enemies. . .

The iree max's Journal state/that a-lermer living near I.imerick, who was "suspected a having paid hi e rent," has had his ears cut off, and been" otherwise barbarously ill-used." The same journal reports the maiming and killing of uttle near Fermov, on land frum which • non-paying tenant had , been evicted. . . . .

The newcomer of terrorism, which is now known as " Boycotting is spreading in all direction.. The limerick Branch of the Land League bee resolved to "Boycott " all solicitors who may venture to appear on behalf of plaintiffs in actions of ejectment or non-payment of rent. A Dublin Coneervative journal states that a " counter- blast "to " Boycotting" in being prepared. It is intended, we are told, to organise a league among English and Scotch farmers for the purpose of .` Boycotting" any Connaught men who maw seek employment in harvest time. The " league " will come to nothing, but the suggention will , probably have occurred to many that "Boymtting " lee I two-edged sword. The Land League agent, at Meath have defeated an at- tempt to cell a farm near Kells. The farm consists of SOO !acres of 'gram land, and an attempt was made to dispose of :it by section. It waspromptly snnouncod that "taking land , toy auction is a violation of the principles of the Irish Land Ledgue." The people were eabortel to away with this insane competition for land," and reminded that "the land ' grabber is an enemy 11 the people." TER GOVERNMENT AND THE LAND LEAOVE.—The Press Assocoation is enabled to state that the Government, having deterniined to place the legality of the I.lnd League policy before the Irish courts for decision, has ito intention of adopting any further meaner, on the subject. Patrick Hoban who acted as herd.. to Captain Boy- cott, having been called upon by the Land League at Claremorris to resign his {magi°, has written to announce that be has resigned in compliance with that request. . . - -

Lerran FROM AN lama LANDLORD.—In a letter received by a Leeds gentleman from Mr. Calverly, a landlord at Kenmare, county Kerry, the writer says I fear we must have a civil war. Terrorism is rampant everywhere. About the quietest place in Ireland no gentleman thinks of going out unharmed, and very few peasants care ta be out after dusk. There is mo security for life or property. Those who belong to the movement can openly that there will be a revolution during the next two months. Christmas was the time pradicted as long ago or M.ty last. Ord help those who remain in the country at that time." Tim IRIS!! LAND LEAGUE IN AMERICA. Branchec of the Irish Land League have been established at Concord, New Hampshire, laud Lawrence, Massachusetts: the organi- sation at the latter place being presided over by A Korean Catholic priest. Bloom the Sultan is fairly out of P. diplomatic I intrigue another starts up in which he can further exporimentalies in political ingglery. For over two yearn be has practised all the devices of proornatina• lion to cajole the principal Cabinets of Europe into rendering the Berlin Treaty waste paper, but hie strategire have failed him, and, distrusted by every Esropean Government, be has had to yield through mereion the port of Detain° to the Montenegrins. Now he is confronted by the Greeks, armed to the teeth, demanding redreaa by a re•arraegement of frontier, and by the claims of the Berlin Congreaa for an anwlioration of the condition of the Artneatiaes. The farce in which his sublime Majeaty sought to play off the obatinsey of the Albanian League against the demands of the Great Power. of Europe for the surrender of Dolcigno to the Montenegrins IA to be rehearsed by the Ottoman Horde whenever the States, which were partiee to the Berlin Treaty, shall prom for the execution of reform. in Armenia. To pat the Ottoman Km& into an ostensible position of °baloney and a determination to resist the execution of the promieed reforms, the Turidah Government haa fur- nished them with Martini• Henry rifles. These Horde, however, are turning their rifle, to other use. than to simply defending the present syatem of Government in Armenia, for the Persian troops find themselves face to face with these very warriora in their endeavour to quell the rebellion of the Persian Kurds, and the Shah is wrath with the Sultan and his advisers. The pretiding genius at the court of Teheran doe. 110 t attempt to mince matters in lits protest against what he describee am thee trencher. man policy" of Conetantinople, for he aocuaee the Sultan of having broken hi, solemn promise to ban that he would so protect the Ottoman frontier as to prevent the Ottoman Kurds from creasing the Fenian line, and joining the Persian Herd.; and he VOW 3 that, so far as Penis is eon- caned, Turkey may perish. Here are the genes of a pritty wriouti quarrel, which may develop into active hostiiities between the Courte of Teheran and Constantinople, and bring abuit a fresh and a very serious complication in Asintic politico. Ai present Penae hat her hands full in auppreeeing her Kurdish ' rebellions subjects and re reacting the Ottoman Herds who have run over her borders. Russia cannot close her eye• to the in/narration of the belligerenoe who are laying waste sone of the remote parts of the Shah', kingdom, and which, if it proved suocessful, would lead to the eetalffiahment of a aparate Kurdish State too near to the confines of &Wei= territory to be agrepfre to the Government a Bt. Petersburg. It was feared at one time that the Shah would be driven to court the aid of Russia., suppress the rebel- lion, and then would have arisen an increseed watelt. kiln, as and suspicion in pedal. Astati,. Hitherto, however, the Persian royal troops have been able to cope with the rebels, but the latter are still active and ate finding the Shahla seldiere much work. The rebela are led by a fiurdieh chief named Obsidtath, who has grant influence over his follower. He is looked upon an a asnefierionious personage, and is hold in high veneration. Coupled with has sanctity is ambi• don, and some time ago he openly roasted the suthority of the Sultan. When he had settled his differences with His Majesty, he found attractions beyond the Persian frontier, aud joined the rebels at the head of 8,000 men, whom he had suoceeded

ST. HELEN' LITERARY AND SCIEN- TIFIC ASSOCIATION. On Tuesday night, an elaborete and well-written paper wee read before the member, of this asseciation,by Or. Hey, oil The Curiosities of Langulge." Mr. F. J. Allen, in the Absence of the president, occupied the chair. At the clo. of the tamper, the Rev. Canon Carr mid that if he untle.tood the lecturer that language had gone on gradually developing as mind develope,l from childhood, he confessed some diffi- culty iu accepting that authority, from the very fact that the very bent examplee they had of the beauties of language were not to be found in the modern developments referred to so beautifully and cle.trly lay the lecturer. They had had only one Homer in the world, and he lived in a very remote period indeed. Croieg back la the Homan Empire from Cicero, and back to the Greek from Dernowhenee, we would expect in the efforts of our modern poets and modern auditors aomething far exceeding anything we had found in the old writing.. But they did not 6.1 that. And although science in it, various applications from modern exercises had brought out wonderful things. yet for the great prin.' ciplex of science they had to go very far bade in I Cue ages. Our English language was the greatest in the world, and he understood the lecturer to i can the fullest language to the world, but he I did not think their German friends would be vett' men, obliged to the lecturer for intimating that if we advanced in our English language we should altogether di,card Germo, John Bright, the late Biehop of Chester, and come of our best speakers were in the habit of using the purest Saxon, and in proportion AS men spoke the purest Saxon, would they make the meet illustrious and efficient orators. If that be correct, they they would scarcely be right in sop- posing that in order to make more perfect their language they most be continually be making new development, With regard to the origin ef language, he had never heard sny account of the origin or probable origin of languages which set snide, or was calculated to interfere in the lewd degree with the eccounts given in the Old Book. In Genetic they had an account of the origin and of diversity of lan. guages on the faco of the earth. How the ramification of those languages went on it was impossible for them to tell. He believed the gift of speech, or of language, in the tirst instanee, was given by God, who made at the same time the human mind as distinct from every other thing created: and the only account they Lad given them with regard to the diversity of languages eras given them in the hietory of the Tower of Babel. -o ' .

Mr. Secrrr alno spoke, and agreed with theniew expressed , by the Rev. Canon Carr as to the gift of language being the gift of God, bet the more they exercised it the more perfect would n become. But they found in the Greek language I the noblest production next to the Bible. They were a highly intellectual race. and they had a beautiful climate. They had more time to mad and understand their language, and they committed to memory and repeated their father's sayings. which they handed down from one generation to another.

The Rev. 51E10.11015M proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, with whom he agreed that the English language would become the language of the world. The English, Isrignage had, perhaps, more than any other ...imitated itself to the Greek language. Some of the most forcible, he said. and perhaps some of the most beautiful orations at the present day were in the English language but they mold , not be expressed on concisely as in mine other languages,

..... The Rev J. P. Racnto seconded the motion. and in the course of his speech mid that no doubt the poetry of Homer : was very grand and perfect in ifawn,, but for a description of mental processes they looked in vain. They had grand natural scenery and outward action, hut nothing of the workings of the human mind or motions of the human heart.

Widnes,which we.' mere collection of. few houses emcee of years ago, at a time when the border. of our river were occupied with the elite of such towns Ic Manchester, who seat their first familiea to Runcorn, which wa, noted as a watering place. But the terrible smell. from Widnes have moiled all that, and mimed nearly every green enrolt which wo were justly proud, at that time. I felt one ur two inches taller on reading your journal, and observing that my old friend, Mr. George Marshall, had raid at one of the meetings held oo the subject that "it 1.11 high time they had the honour of entertaining the supporters of the society.. and bringing thenmelves into closer contact with the nobility, gentry, and agricultural intermt of khe county." tM,,rearl- ieg this, and seeing that my old friend bad Finch "a soul above buttons," and was anxious to mingle with the nobility, wy heart fairly bounded whine me, for I IMIAI ronf., like .any Itrtfishers, that I have • little of • weaknesa for a real lord." The meeting memed to go off mpitally, and on heuing bow successful the promoters of the mheme had been at the public meeting held at the Commissioners' Boarderoom, on Monday, my heart almost leaped romp mouth at the prospect of having my wish. realised. A deputation was appointed to wait on the mremitte• of the rwelety at the annual meeting, which took place at Creweon Wednesday and I must say I felt sorry fur the p,or fellows when I saw them return in rho afternoon, all looking as solemner, owls. Even ray lolly friend, the former Mayor of the town—l hope no one will think I allude to any one but Mr. Norman—failed to smile, and Mr. Wm. Handley w. as sober as lobe had just been to a foneral. The tale was • very brief one—they had lost by two vote.. I button-holed members o( rho deputation separate,y some short time after- wards,and Ire backbiting I heard wassomethingdreadful. Our blamed this thing and another the other, but the majority aoincidel in the view that too many "cocks" had spoiled the show "broth." In a multitude of counsellors there is said tube wisdom, but the members of the deputation said that the multitude of talkers bat simply ruined their chances. It seems that Mr. Wm. Handley won "the blue ribbon," and was appointed to barbs chief speaker when the deputa- tion were introduced to the erecting. His brief speech is Mated to have done good ; bet mv friend "George" made a terrible slip when he put in his "-oar," which he was plainly toll to lift out of the rowlocks for the occasion, and stated that he had been waited upon by the publimns of the town of Ron,rn, who had urged him to do all in his power to get , the show there, and promised that if he were successful in ee doing, they would undertake to go round with snurrrh.e ref email eubscriptien books and "raise the wind." I atn told by eome of the viairors that or soon as Mn Marshall had in- troduced the publicsne on the scene, in the way of patronisers el the committee, it was found that more of thern began to change couMenance, and from that moment the case went against Runcorn. Then, Mr. Norman could not he quiet, bet he must hen.". word." and that meam opening the oodgates of talk. I can assure you, Mr. Editor, I feel in a , sad way at the result, especially after all the fuss and excite-I meat which there has been in Runcorn on this matter during , the last few days. As far act am concerned, I have done with agricultural shows for the future—l anr, yours, he., I %mown, 25th Nov., 1860. MANGEL-WURZEL.

On Toes-day M-o-rUh;gy ÜbTaleOi7ork-W.n-roPened at the tipper Portlandsetreet Congregational Church Schoolroom, Southport, the object being to obtain fend, for the liquida- tion of the debt yet remaining on the building. J. hi McMintetes, NIT. for Warrington, who was received with much applause. said he had heard the object for which the bazaar or the sale of work was being opened, and he must exprem hie tope that the expectations of his friends would be realised. He bad been told that the people nailed that a sale of work because they objected partly to the came of bagmr and partly to tome accompaniments often found therewith. Especidly, lie h.l been told, that they objected to what wan called "raffling," nod that they did not intend to have anything of the kind there. (Hear, hoar, and applause.) He enact at once confess that he slid not join with the objections. lie believed that bazaars Were a very excellent way of raining funds for charitable and religioue purposee; and he believed, moreover, that the ob- jection, which obhtin.l against bazaars were remnant, of old memories when, perhaps, there really were objections— ae when extortianato prices were charged—wbea a good deal of disagreeable importunity was practised—or when, paha'', there want mild kind of what censorioun people would call gambling. lint he must say that he never saw anything but whet roomed to be extremely innocent. The Bishop of Liverpool wan at a laimar two or three weeks ago, and if the people elm got it up contemplated that his lordahip would speak very favourably of it thi y were much disappointed, for hie lonlehip blemsed tbe means with very faint praise inslool. lie said :—" Amongst those thin, connected with bazaar% which he disliked most were raffle, beeavee he Ives pereuaded they led to the habit of gambling, which proved a curse to many noble houses in England and Wright them to ruin. That this habit was due to raffles there could be no doubt. Ile was persuaded there was in Liverpm: already too much gambling—it was immetimee called speculation—in cotton and other edictre of commerce, and he did not wish to encourage any practice that would lead up to it." Nobody here approved of gambling—theory hear)—nut the Bishop put the matter a little too strongly and illogically when he 3411 the habit of gambling was no doubt due to raffles at bazaars. Perhaps he alluded to such oases of which that of t' e Marquis of Hastings was a type. Bat he (the speaker) did not believe the dfarquis acquired hi, habile of gambling at bazaars. He doubted whether that nobleman ever attended a ante of work of Chic kind. He I did not believe in the exietence of any connection of bazaars with cotton speculations. However, there was no raffling here, snd there was no cause for them to biome themaelves. They would not be troubled at the end of the proceedings I with some vague fear of having given the impetus to 8..31 one which would lead to hirer her ruin. Dr. Byte hod also I a great objection to pin cushione and antimacassars. His ' observation was that "it would be much better to selll articles that were uneful. A man might buy a goo I shirt— (laughter)—a good coat, era goal pair of Ape, lie could : rot fill hie house with pincushions ; and as to antienacomm. they were always sticking to the buttons of a man's coat". Haverthelme pincushions were very useful, and might ' be pretty without being ten, so. Antimacassars might be very ornamental, and the habit of stickieg to 3 man's butte, was not acquired at bazaars. (laughter.) He had no doubt there were many ladies present who could make a Inana good shirt. but the man must be very exact- ing who would like to have the practical experience of a coat eta pair of shoes made by any lady preeent (Hear, hear.) But hia lorilehip's net blanket did not quite cover' the inetitationy for he said that—. No doubt these gatherings had their goal points in the matter of miring money for religion,' and philanthropic purposes, and for tl.at they ought no doubt to feel thankful." Therein he agreed with Ids lordship. .Ilendrols of charitable and religion, objects would net have achieved their present success but for the pecuniary assistance derived from those kind of sales. Meer, boar.) He had been connected with such institutioos for nmre than thirty years; and when he recollected the cnod done, the dintress relieved, the poverty alleviated, the orance enlightened, and the religious instruction im- parted, he could not but with them success. It was bO3lO. timee said that those who worked for such sales had not that singleness and parity of motive which ought to actuate them. He did not believe this, became he had seen young men and young women work with a zeal which showed they had a proper appreciation of the ebjectn for which they were labouring. The Bishop of Liverpool had some advice to give to young Indies. lie said .--" lie would like to my to young ladies who had taken no much pine with the hector, that they might ale° fled 'Hai of usefalnem in Sunday echool work, district vikiting, and looking after the wants of other,. He said this to show the young !Aim that there were many goal and useful things to be done in the world besides, attending at bazaars. He hoped the time would come when Christian people would not need to raise money for religious objects hy means of bazaara. but would give what they could when they knew (two, wanted, and that in time young ladle. attending to bazmre would go out of fashion altogether." But district s 'siting and Sundae school teach- ing were not every lady's vocation. Seine had not the healthy the ability, or the courage. And tote giving independently to baaaars that begged the question altogether. The question was whether in working for bazaars people were not giving In the moot liberal and generous way they could. (Hear, hear.) He remembered being some time ago at a bazaar at Oldham. Home three or four young women there had made • ecreen. It was very beautiful work, and he was fold it was worth £lO. At the sale the article went for £24. Now the young persons had laboured at this etreen a long Sme— lted expended also their skill and haste upon it. The amount obtained was conablerable, but from their condition in life it warn fair presumpbon that they could not have given anything like the num in hard money. In opposition to the Bishop. he hoped the time would not noon come when the attendance of yourgladiesat bazaars would go out of fashion. (Hear, hear.) In reference to their ade of work at that place, he believed the friends wanted te raise £320. His experience was that the promoter,' almost invariably raised more money than they expected, and he did not see why those percent ehoull be exceptional in that respect. CHIMIDIS Flanowartua.—The late Bishop Edward Stanley, of Norwich, while rector of Alderley, half a cen- tury ago, published avow interesting and still popular Faatiliar Hisinry of Bole. fine nature,hlMts,and instinct,. This volume contains many curious anecdotes and reminis- cences of Me personal experience as to the habits of birds in Ms own native country. The following is worth pre- serving —"Atr Dunham, near Altriaclmm, in Cheshire, the seat of the Earl of Stamford, there is a reentry which has enietarl for many Yeam. If happened about the latter end of Mardi, or beginning of April, a few years ago, that a gentleman, riding along the turnpike road, now, in a small field about a mile from the trees where the birds breed, about thirty-five or forty standing on the ground, and occasionally moving slowly in various directions. At first he was um certain what birds they were, a. their heads were thrown hack. anrlashey appeared little raised from the ground ; but, on approaching the spot, he IV, soon Adisfied that they were herons. His presence, however, had no other effect (though in general they are remarkably shy and cautions) than inducing those nearest the hedge. where he hail sta- tioned himself to watch their motions, to walk leisurely to a mote distant part of the field. He remained for wane time a spictator of their singular assemblage, which impres- ser! him with the opinion that it was a deliberate council: and we agree with him that their object wart connected with the usual poring, which takes place about that time. We are the more strengthened in tl e opinion, from haring wit- nessed meetings income degree eimilar amongst other birds." The Bebop then relates similar experiences he had had in connection with float of magpies and starlings.— CoPownt. - . . .

Mr. James Farrington, the inspector of nuisances to the above Authority, has prepared an exhaustive "report and return of siniMry work dons and other matters connected therewith," within the district of the Authority, during the two years ending september 29th lead From this report it appears that the area of the dietrict is 39,773 scres, with • population of 17,953 ; ant the number of townehips under the care of the Authority is 38. The carrying out of the provisions of the Public Health Aet, 1875, entail. a large amount of clerical work. The total numxr of nuisances repotted to the Sanitary Authority was 140,and in connection with these nuisancee, 140 preliminary notices were served by the inspector, verbal oeticee were given by the inspector in 13 cases, and final notices served by order of the Authority in 11 instances. No less than 44 nuisances are retained upon record as unabated. Informationa as to infectious diseases end nuieances were supplied from medical officern of health lathe inspector in 19 cases, and 18 reports were made by the inspector to medical officers. Eleven special reports were furnished by the inspector to the Authority, and 28 complaints were received and regiatered by the in- spector. Coder the denomination of "general nuisances," it was stated that seven dwelling-houses were closed without legal proceedings being taken ; while two were closed by order of the justices. Sixteen dwelling-houses were I reported as overcrowded and afterwards abated, but in three instances proceedings had to be taken to secure an abate- • meet of overcrowding, and in one case it was found necesstry to take proceedings for uon-conspliance with (ustices' order. One dwelling-house was closed upon a second conviction for over-crowding, and one wasimprovtd and rendered fit for habitation. The roofs of 13 dwelling-houses were improved. as woe also the ventilation, and in one rase the inhabitants of a house were living in such a Hibernian tuition that the house had to be cleared of poultry, while in four other caws the nuisinee arising front the keeping of rabbits and poultry! woe abated. laoral proceedings were taken in two instances for the abatement of nuisances, and in each a conviction ' was obtained. A large atnount of information is oleo given under this hea ling respecting. drainage. In accordance with the Public Health (Water) Act, 1878,, total of 84 samplee of water wassubmitted Inc the Inspector , to the County Analyst for analysis Of this number only I seven were returned ee first class waters, and the remainder , were classified as follows:—Second class waters 8, very good , waters 14, good *eters 5, fair waters 4, being of doubtful purity 4, toeing of medium purity 3, toeing contaminated 11, ! had waters 5. The total number of certificates granted for ! the occupation of new houses under the Public Health (Water) Art, 1878, was 23, and 45 houses were or-copied by such of which number 44 were supplied with water. In three instances proceedings were taken for occupying new j houses without first obtaining certificates of occupation from ! the Authority, and a similar number of convictions obtained. ' Dealingleith the water supply of old houses, the report stated that 92 first notices were served by the inspector to • ' provide a water supply. Fifty-seven wcond notices were mood, with the result that forty-three houses were supplied with mater. T.lO schoole were supplied with water from water mains (Warring:on), whilst one public pump was erected by Sanitary Authority; 1 public pump repaired by the Authority ; and 1 public well cleansed. The inspector had disinfectfd three bedrooms and contents after scarlet fever, and a like number was disinfected by order of inspector ' after typhoid fever. Reforting on the Poblic Health (Interments) Act, 1879, Mr. Farrington states that each graveyard or burial ground within the district has been in- spected, and reported upon (with one exception) as being ' satisfactory. A large amnunt of extra work has devolved upon the inspector by the pulsing of the Canal Bea. Act. 1877. Under this Act 489 canal boats were inspacted. For contrarenflun of the Act proceedings were necessitated in 20 caws 17 of which were for using boats as dwellings without ! previously having them registered for such purpose, and three for overcrowding boats. Two summonses were with- drawn, and 18 convictions obtained.

hide dinners are in general not amusing. When they are formed, a they ueually are, of filen who are euppmed to • postai a strong and common sympathy—political, eporting, literary, military, social—there hi nece.,rily a monotony 01 thought and 'feeling, and of the iliaterials which induce thought and feeling. In a male dinner of party politicians. COnversation soon degeneraten into what is termed " shop anealbles about division., criticism of speech., conjectures about iiffice,speculatione on impending election., and above all, that heinous subject on which enormous fibs are ever told, the regietration. Thereat,, however, occasional glimpses in their talk which would ,eein to intimate that they have another life outside the Ile.. of Parliament. But that extenuating circumstane does not apply to the eporting dinner. There they begin with odds and nape, and and end with handicaps and ulds, arid it is doubtful Whether ,it ever wont to any one present, that there is Soy other making combination of atoms thin utile and Bandimps. A dinner of site 6 proverbially a ',dace of Mien.; and the envy and hatred which all literary men really feel for each other, evecially when they are ex- changing dedimtions of mutual Affection, always ensure, in such amemblim, the agreeable presence of a general feeling Of paint ul constraint. If a good thing occurs to a guest, he will not express it, lest his neighbour, who is publi,hing a novel in numbers, shall appropriate it next month, or he himself, who h, the same responsibility of production, be deprived of its legitimate appearance. Thom who deaire to learn something at the maineuvreo of the Russian and Pros- Sian rev iiws, or the last rumour at Aldershot or the military Chiba, will know where to find this feast of reason. 'The flow of soul in these male festivals 6 perhaps, on the whole, more genial when found iitaeocivtv of young gentlemen, graduates of the Turf and the Marlborough, and guided in their benigiard studies by the gentle experience and the mild wisdom of White's. The Marching scandal, the rat- tling anecidet-, the astounding leaps, and the amazing shot., afford for Ito,ooeeerf,raintewhat pleasing distraction, but when it is diaeorereil that all thme habitual aim-llama are, In general, the airy creatures of inaccuracy and exaggera- tion—that the scandal is not true, the anecdote hoe no foundation, and that the feate of skill and strength are In- vested with the organic windiness of tradition, the vagaries Ime something of the charm of novelty, and are almost as ineipid 311 claret from whi,h the bouquet hen evaporated.— ..Ea/anion " by the Earl of Beaconvteld.

THE ANTI ,C RN LAW AGITATION. he condlinn of Engiand at the meeting of Parliament in 1 2 was not satistactory. The depresaion of trade in the of ..cturing districts seemed over whel ming,and continued InCreasing during the whole of the year. A memorial from Stockport to the Queen in the spring represented that more than half the master spinners h.' failed, nod that no less tlmn three thousand dwelling-houses were untenanted. One. fifth of the population of Leeds were dependent on the poor. rates. The state of Sheffield was not less severe ; end the blast furnaces of IVolvertumonni were extinguished. There Were almost daily meetings at Liverpool, Mthrhester, and Leeds to rmsider the great and increasing distreee of the country, and to induce Ministers to bring forward remedial rteasores ; but as these were impossible, violence was sass nAbstitoted for passionate appeals to the fears or the hunsanity of the Government. Vast bodies of the population taaambled in Stalyhridge nod Ashton and Oldham, and marched into Manchester. . . . . . .

For a week the rioting was unchecked, but the Govern- Ment despatched a etrong military force to that city, and order was restored. The state of affairs in Scotland was not more favourable. There were food note in several of the Scotch tow, and in Glasgow the multitude assembled, aml then commenced What they called a 'Rigging tour, but which was really A progress of not diaguised intimidation. The economic crisis 1,, Ireland was yet to corne, but the whole of that country waa absorbed in a harassing and dangerous agitation for the repeal of the union between the two countries. During all this time the Anti-Corn LAW Lomita was hold- ing regular and frequent meeting. at Manchwiter, at which statements were made diktingufshed by great eloquence and littic scruple. But the aide leaders of this confederacy never succeeded in enlisting the sympathies of the great body of Me population. Between the m:kkters and the workmen . there Wila An alienation of feeling, which apparently never cool Ibe removed. This rererve, however,did not enlist the working classes on the aide of the Government then had their own object, and one which they themselves enthu- dastically cherished. And this woo the Charter, a political settlentent which WAR to restore the golden age, arid which the master manufacturers and the middle classes generally looked upon with evi.n more apprehension than her Majesty'. advisers. tale hardly necessary to add, that inc eta. of affairs like that which 111 here faintly but still faithfully sketch ed , the rapid diminution of the revenue was inevit- able, and, of course, that decline mainly occurrtd in the two all-importint branch,e of the Cuatum, and Excise. Them was another great misfortune, al., which at this trying time hung over England. The country wmdejected. The humiliating disasters of Afghanistan, dark narratives Of which were periodically arriving, hail rwoduced eater, depresaing effect on the spirit of the country than all the victories and menaces of Napoleon in the heyday of his wild career. At home and abroad there mewed nothrng to sus- tain the national spirit financial embarrassment, commer- cial and manufacturing distress,social and political agitation on the one hand, and on the other the loss of armies, of repo. lotion, perhaps of empire. It was true that these external misfortunes could hardly he attributed to the new Ministry, —but when a nation i.e thoroughly perplexed and dispirited it mon ceases to make distinctions between political parties. The country is out of sorts, and the " Government " is held answerable for the dimrder.—. Feriyaion" lat the Earl of Bearonrfeltl. _ .

div.p: THE ST. HELENS MAGISTRATES AND THE EDUCATION AND NUNES REGU- LATION ACTS.

A— CAM of much interest was clecirled at the St. Helens Police Court by the magiwratek, Meet.. W. L. Eva. and Willis, on Monday last. Thomas Pen- oington, a collier, was summoned for neglecting to send hie eon to school. A few weeks ago Pennindon's ease was ad• journed, Mr. Swift, who annear.l for him, stating that Pet,-' oington did not want to violate the law, but he, with a number of others, were anxious to have it decided whether the Mines Regulation Act, 1872, overrode the Education Act of 1870. Mn. Suencely announced that he would consider t innestion, and the case was then adjourned. The St. Here. School Attendance Committee at their last meeting expressed a desire to have the question settled, though they would not fleecier:ally accept the decision of a Bench of longterm. as final. Atr. Thom, solicitor, on Monday , appeared on behalf of the School Attendance Committee,anil said that the bye-law, of the committee, which they were ! empowered to make, comprised one which enacted that the pae,nentererynirilrt of mere thou five and lese than thirteen years of age should rouse such child to attend school unlese there were reaso.ble excuses for non-attendance, and he said that in the Coal Mines Regulation Act there was no provision made for the eflucatien of children working and:: that Act after they hart attained the age of twelve

Mr. Swift, in adDessing the Bench, said the inspector of the St. Helens district had supplied to the collieries through- out the whole of the district an alertract showing the opinion of the Secretary of State and inspector, an follows Pasa- graph 18—Women and girls of any age mav not be employed at all (meaning enderground). Paragraril; li—Boye under twelve shell not be employed at all unless the mine is specially exempted be the Secretary of State by reason of the thinness of the seam, but subject to certain conditions elated in the exemption boys between ten and twelve may lon employed. Paragraph IS—Boys of twelve awl under 13, and male young persons of 13 and under lii may be em- ployed not more than 5-1 shoos a week and mom than ten hours a day, and are to be allowed an interval of twelve hours ter rest between two consecutive period, of employment, ex- cept between Friday and Saturday, when an interval of eight hours will suffice." Mr. Swift contend.4l that it was quite clear from the Act that it regulated the education of boys employed in mines, not it was quite clmr that, while it adipulated for a certain amount of education for boys under twelve, it distinctly Minuted Imys over twelve to put in full time and require no education at all. The magistrates consulted in private, and, on returning, Mr. Evans sail thee hot decided to convict, though they had had some difficulty in coming to a decision. They considered, looking at the Coal Mines Regulation Set care- fully, that there was no provision there for the .4:cation of children over twelve years of age, and they were of opinion that the Education Acts of 1876 and 18.90 intend.] to pro- vide foe the further education of children. They considered them was a difference between themes of Mellor r. Denham, cited by Mr. Swift, that case being under the Factory Acts, and theee Acts provid.al for tlie education of children up to 14 years of age. Mr. Swift mid be should advise his client to act in accordance with their Worships' judgment, and send the child to school. . . . . .

Brown, on Ireland, since the conquest." Dr. McNicol occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Brown, in his preliminary retnark, stated that the paper was not intended to provoke political discussion, but was rather a resume of the tearing facia of hiatory in relation to Ireland since iM conquest by this country ; to that the members might be better fitted for accurately entering upon a discussion on Irish affairs. Mr. Brown sketched the condition of Ireland immediately prior to the conquest by Homy the Second, remarking that it was Wooer than in the time of the heptarchy The kings were constantly quarrelling, and the country Which ahOuld have provided bread for the poor was desolated by wars, and the people were obliged to pay enormous tributes to carry them , on. The land was crowded with churchmen, for we found , that there were no less than 300 bishops in the year 1152. Having spoken of the apportionment of land resulting from the conquest, he eaid the misfortunes of the country from the date of the couqueat seemed to be multiplied. English kings often troubled with difficulties at home found it to he the easiest way to govern Ireland by sending. succession of adventurers whom chief object was plunder. Ile commented upon the anarchy to. confulirm prevelont during the reigns of the whale of the Plantageneta, and s tid during the wars of the Roses !lie great Anglo.lrish chief- tains generally took the WO of the Yorkist, but from the l'ieculiar position of the country tlodr efforta gene- ' rally tended to their own aggrandisement, rather than to the helping of any claimant to the throne of England. The measure. of Henry VIII. were disliked none because he interfered with the authority of the Pope than from any change he made in the form of worship. The new Liturgy under Edward VI. provoked great jealousy, but under Mary the English government of Ireland was more in harmony with Irish views on the sub- ject of religion.
